Meet Teambrella, the first peer-to-peer insurance service powered by Bitcoin

Hi!

After a year of work we’re out of stealth mode. We believe that our system sets up a new very high standard of fairness and transparency that is unachievable by any insurance company that is not cryptocurrency-based. We’re currently polishing the system so an alpha will probably be ready in Q2.

Our white paper (it’s only 17 pages): http://teambrella.com/whitepaper.pdf

The tl;dr version of our white paper:

  • Alignment of interests: Insurance companies and policyholders have conflict of interests. We propose a peer-to-peer insurance organization devoid of this conflict.

  • Teams: Anyone can create a new team. Existing members decide who they want in their team.

  • Voting: Everything in a team is governed via voting. The weight of a teammate's vote depends on premiums she has paid.

  • Liquid Democracy: Teammates can delegate their votes to proxies. Those who do vote receive a reward so they can do this professinally.

  • Risk Coefficients: Each teammate is assigned a risk coefficient by the team via discussion and voting.

  • Fair P2P Coverage: If two teammates have same risk coefficients they cover each other for the same amount. If one is less risky, e.g. a good driver, she gets more coverage from the other.

  • Distributed Wallets: A multi-sig wallet controlled by the owner AND 3 out of 8 of his teammates. Wallet owner can veto any transaction. He is allowed to withdraw funds provided all outstanding premiums can be paid out. We coordinate payments but it's teammates who really make them.

  • Protection: Our open-source client software allows teammates to collectively withdraw their funds if the server is compromized or shutdown.

This is all really cool stuff! There's a few issues I see with it currently though. If you're talking health insurance, how can these teams make sure their plans are ACA compliant? That's a big problem in the realm of health insurance, as you CAN have a plan that isn't ACA compliant, but if you do, you still have to pay the pretty hefty fine for not having insurance, as it doesn't count.

Would that be something left up to the teams, or would your group(corp/team/what?) be able to assist with that? I mean, it's not HARD to get your plan to be ACA certified, as all you have to do is present your plans to the Insurance commissioner of the state you intend to sell your plan in. S/he tells you if your plan is ACA certified, and approves how much you can sell your plan for.

The other issue is that outside of very specific circumstances, if you intend to sell ACA certified plans, you MUST do so during the Open Enrollment Period which s November 1st to January 31st. It's actually against federal law to sell them outside that period without a customer having what are called Qualifying Life Events, which are worded VERY specifically, so there's literally no misinterpretation of them.

As an example, say you lost your employer coverage: You have Sixty(60) days from the day that your employer coverage ends to purchase a new plan. When you go to apply, you must provide documentation stating explicitly that your coverage ends on this day, and that your employer is no longer covering you.

Not that you don't know all of this, but if you're planning on allowing health insurance teams, it's definitely something to keep in mind.

Source: Sell Aetna health insurance for a living.

It's actually the best strategy in terms of expected value. But the worst in terms if variance.
Can you elaborate on that a little more, please?
You're "losing money" with any insurance in the long run. But this loss of money buys you a lower variance aka peace of mind.
So you're saying saving will not accumulate enough money to pay for what most people need insurance for if they start saving at the same time they would've started paying for insurance?

Most people put in more than they take out. But a few people have horrible things happen to them and so they might take out a lot more than they put in. Everyone is happy because nobody wants to have something horrible happen and NOT be able to afford the bills.

Think home insurance. Are you happy with your insurance even if your house never burns down and so you never get any money back? Yes, because if your house were to burn down, you'd be covered. If you had been setting your own money aside all that time, you would have had to put a lot more money in. (Home insurance obviously doesn't cost as much as your house burning down would) This all works because houses burning down is rare. Everyone pools their money to cover the people who have expensive but unlikely shit happen to them, which is a net monetary loss for most, but a gain in peace of mind for everyone.
So "variance" means how much money is available sooner?

Yeah that's part of it. It's also protection against the case where something so unexpectedly bad happens that it turns out you weren't saving enough money all along.

Really he is using word variance as a statistical term. Mean is the average of some values, and variance is how spread out they are. So 10,10,10,10,10 has mean of 10 and zero variance. 0,5,10,15,20 also happens to have mean of 10, but has a larger variance. There is a formula for calculating variance that you can look up.

The cost of real life disasters have very high variance. You could get hit with some medical condition that costs millions or what have you. So your bills could look like 0,0,10,0,1000000, with that million being very unlikely but still possible.

But if you take a huge pool of people, some small percentage of those people will always be getting hit by such catastrophes, so it is more consistent (lower variance). That's how, with insurance, your expenses can be consistent (low variance), but you will end up paying more (higher mean) than you would have if you had paid out of pocket. Unless you are one of the unlucky few who experience costly unexpected disasters (they end up paying less than if they had gone uninsured and paid out of pocket).
